textbookText: Josef Stefan was born to Slovenian parents in St. Peter, Austria, and he graduated from the university of Vienna in 1857. At the University of Vienna, he rose from lecturer in mathematical physicist in 1858 to professor Ordinarius of physics in 1863 and to the director of the Physical Institute in 1866. Five years after he derived his law of black body radiation empirically, it was derived theoretically by Ludwig Boltzmann of Austria, and hence became known as the Stefan-Boltzmann law. Stefan- Boltzmann law states that the radiant energy of a black body (a theoretical object that absorbs all radiation that falls on it) is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature. This law was one of the first important steps toward the understanding of the black body which gave the base for the quantum idea of radiation.
1. When a coil of copper is kept at a certain distance above the flame of a candle, the candle keeps burning, but when the coil is placed over the flame, it is extinguished.
2. Tanks of gasoline are generally painted with aluminum paints. 3. The earth constantly receives heat radiations from the sun and gets warmed up. 4. Water can be boiled in a paper cup.
